title: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 16 Startup Metrics
text:
## Bookings vs Revenue
Bookings is the value of a contract between the company and the customer, reflecting a contractual obligation to pay. Revenue is recognized when the service is actually provided or ratably over the life of the subscription, and is governed by GAAP. Letters of intent and verbal agreements are neither bookings nor revenue. Do not conflate the two.

## Recurring Revenue: ARR and MRR
ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) measures the revenue components that are recurring in nature, and should exclude one-time (nonrecurring) fees and professional service fees. ARR per customer should be flat or growing; if it is shrinking the company has upsell/cross-sell or churn problems. MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is monthly recurring revenue. A frequent mistake is to multiply one single month's bookings by 12 to derive ARR, because this improperly counts one-time and professional-services fees, and assumes the whole month's bookings are recurring.

## Gross Profit
Gross profit includes all of the costs associated with making, delivering, and supporting a product/service (cost of goods sold), not just a headline revenue figure.

## TCV vs ACV
Total Contract Value (TCV) is the total value of the contract, and can be shorter or longer in duration; it includes one-time charges, professional service fees, and recurring charges. Annual Contract Value (ACV) is the value of the contract over a 12-month period.

## LTV (Lifetime Value)
LTV is the present value of the future net profit from the customer over the duration of the relationship. It helps determine the long-term value of a customer and how much value is generated per acquisition dollar. Steps: (1) revenue per customer per month = average order value times number of orders; (2) contribution margin per customer = revenue from the customer minus variable costs associated with that customer; (3) average customer lifespan in months = 1 divided by monthly churn rate; (4) LTV = contribution margin per customer times average customer lifespan. Use contribution margin (not revenue) so you account for the cost to serve. A conservative approach uses 12- and 24-month historical LTV rather than projecting an infinite lifespan.

## GMV vs Revenue (marketplaces)
Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) is the total sales dollar volume of merchandise transacting through the marketplace in a period. Revenue is the portion of GMV that the marketplace takes: transaction fees, advertising, sponsorships and so on. GMV is not revenue.

## Deferred Revenue and Billings
Deferred revenue is cash collected in advance of the service being delivered, and is booked as a liability on the balance sheet. Because ARR/revenue alone can hide slowing sales, use billings: Billings = current-period revenue + (current-period deferred revenue minus prior-period deferred revenue). Growing billings is a stronger health signal than revenue alone.

## CAC: Blended vs Paid
Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) is fully loaded acquisition spend divided by new customers acquired. Blended CAC divides total acquisition cost by total new customers across all channels (including organic). Paid CAC divides acquisition cost by only the customers acquired through paid marketing. The danger of blended CAC is that it hides how much it actually costs to acquire a customer via paid channels, because organic customers drag the average down. Investors want paid CAC (and CAC by channel) to judge whether growth scales profitably. Include all costs: referral fees, credits, discounts.

## Active Users, CMGR, Churn, Burn
Define active users precisely so accidental or one-time users are not counted. Use CMGR (compounded monthly growth rate) = (latest month / first month)^(1/number of months) minus 1 rather than a simple average of month-over-month rates. Churn: monthly unit churn = customers lost / prior-month total; gross MRR churn = MRR lost / beginning-of-period MRR; net revenue churn = (MRR lost minus MRR from upsells) / beginning MRR. Burn rate is the rate at which cash decreases: gross burn is total monthly cash outflows (expenses), net burn is gross burn minus revenue (net cash consumed per month).

## Presentation Anti-Patterns
Downloads are a vanity metric; prefer engagement (DAU/MAU, sharing). Cumulative charts (cumulative revenue, users, bookings) can go up-and-to-the-right even when a business is shrinking, so they are not valid growth measures. Avoid chart tricks: unlabeled or truncated Y-axis, exaggerated scaling, percentages shown without absolute numbers. Good metrics serve operating decisions, not just a fundraising narrative.

title: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 16 More Startup Metrics
text:
## TAM: Bottom-Up, Not Top-Down
Total Addressable Market should be built bottom-up: start from the target customer profile, realistic willingness to pay, and the actual go-to-market/distribution strategy, then sum up. Top-down calculation (take a giant population and assume a penetration percentage) tends to overstate market size because it ignores distribution realities. The classic error is 'if we sell a toothbrush to 40% of China.' Bottom-up forces you to reason through the real channels (drugstores, grocery, online).

## ARR pitfalls and GMV vs Revenue
ARR is recurring revenue on an annual basis, excluding one-time fees, professional services, and variable usage fees. A common mistake is multiplying one month's recognized bookings by 12 to get ARR. For marketplaces, GMV (what consumers spend) is not Revenue (the marketplace's take).

## ARPU
Average Revenue Per User = total revenue divided by number of users for a specific period (month, quarter, or year). Pre-revenue or early companies are often benchmarked against an established competitor's ARPU. The post cites Facebook U.S./Canada ARPU of $9.30 in FY2015 Q2 as an example.

## Gross Margins and Benchmarks
Gross margin = total sales revenue minus cost of goods sold, as a percentage of revenue. Benchmark examples: e-commerce (Amazon) around 27%; software companies should target 80% to 90%. The intuition for software's high margin: 'Software is something I have, I can sell it to you, and I still have it,' meaning near-zero marginal cost to serve an additional customer.

## Sell-Through and Inventory Turns
Sell-through rate = units sold in a period divided by items at the beginning of the period (also called close rate, conversion rate, or success rate in a marketplace). Inventory turns = cost of goods sold for a period divided by average inventory for the period. Managing inventory too tightly to boost turns can hurt sales.

## Network Effects, Virality, Economies of Scale
Network effects mean the product gets more valuable as more people use it; there is no single metric that proves them (OpenTable evidenced them via rising rep productivity, diners seated, direct-booking share, and declining restaurant churn). Virality is measured by the viral coefficient (k) = average invitations sent times the invite-to-user conversion rate; k > 1 is viral, k < 1 is not. Example: 1,000 users each send 5 invites (5,000), 15% convert (750 new) gives k = 0.75, not viral. Economies of scale mean unit cost decreases as output grows; this is distinct from virality and network effects.

## NPS, Cohort Analysis, Registered vs Active Users
Net Promoter Score asks 'how likely are you to recommend us to a friend' on a 0 to 10 scale; NPS = percent Promoters (9 to 10) minus percent Detractors (0 to 6). Do not survey only power users (biased sample) and do not compare NPS across companies; watch your own trend. Cohort analysis tracks groups who signed up in the same period over time; you want retention to stabilize after 6 to 12 months and newer cohorts to perform better than older ones. Registered users is a cumulative metric that can go up-and-to-the-right even as the business shrinks, and is easily gamed; active users (DAU/WAU/MAU, and the DAU-to-MAU engagement ratio) are the honest counterpart.

## Customer Concentration Risk and Presentation
Customer concentration = largest customer's revenue divided by total revenue; lower is safer because a single dominant customer gains pricing leverage. Presentation anti-patterns: truncating the Y-axis (always baseline at zero) and reporting revenue, users, or bookings cumulatively (which masks decline).

title: David Skok (forEntrepreneurs), SaaS Metrics 2.0: A Guide to Measuring and Improving What Matters
text:
## The Two Guiding Unit-Economics Rules
David Skok reduces SaaS viability to two guardrails. First, the LTV to CAC ratio: the best SaaS businesses have an LTV to CAC ratio higher than 3, sometimes as high as 7 or 8. Second, the time to recover CAC: aim to recover CAC in 5 to 7 months. Profitability is anemic if the time to recover CAC extends beyond 12 months. These two together determine whether a SaaS business can fund its own growth; a strong LTV to CAC with slow CAC recovery still creates a cash-flow trough that must be financed.

## LTV Formulas
CAC = total Sales and Marketing expenses divided by the number of new customers acquired in the period. In early stages, adjust for expensive team members who have not yet scaled, or CAC will read artificially high. Simple LTV (consistent ARPA, no expansion) = ARPA divided by Customer Churn Rate. LTV including gross margin = ARPA times Gross Margin percent, divided by Customer Churn Rate. Including gross margin (per Ron Gill of NetSuite) reveals a big lever on LTV/CAC worth focusing on, because a customer's true value is the margin they generate, not their revenue.

## Months to Recover CAC
Months to recover CAC = CAC divided by (ARPA times Gross Margin percent). The guideline is under 12 months, though land-and-expand enterprise businesses now often run around 20 months. The LTV to CAC guideline of greater than 3 assumes a gross margin of roughly 80 percent or higher when using the simpler LTV formula without a margin adjustment.

## Churn and Negative Churn
If Net Revenue Churn is high (above 2 percent per month) it indicates something is wrong in the business. The most powerful growth lever is negative net revenue churn, where expansion revenue from the existing base exceeds revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades. Skok illustrates that reaching about minus 3 percent net revenue churn produces dramatically higher revenue than a positive-churn business over the same window, because the installed base grows on its own before any new customers are added. Negative churn is what lets the best SaaS companies compound.

## Why These Matter
The deeper point of SaaS Metrics 2.0 is that a SaaS business looks unprofitable early precisely because acquisition costs are paid up front while revenue arrives over the customer lifetime. Understanding the cash trough, the months-to-recover-CAC, and LTV to CAC lets a founder distinguish a business that is losing money because it is broken from one that is losing money because it is investing in profitable growth.

title: David Sacks (Craft Ventures), The Burn Multiple
text:
## Definition and Formula
The Burn Multiple = Net Burn divided by Net New ARR. It measures how much a startup is burning in order to generate each incremental dollar of ARR. Net Burn is cash revenue minus cash operating expenses (the actual net cash consumed in the period). Net New ARR = New ARR plus Expansion ARR minus Churned ARR (the true change in ARR over the same period). The higher the Burn Multiple, the more the startup is burning to achieve each unit of growth; the lower the Burn Multiple, the more efficient that growth is.

## The Rating Table
Sacks gives a simple grading scale for venture-stage startups: Burn Multiple under 1x is Amazing, 1x to 1.5x is Great, 1.5x to 2x is Good, 2x to 3x is Suspect, and over 3x is Bad. A company burning less than one dollar for every new dollar of ARR is exceptionally efficient; a company burning more than three dollars per new ARR dollar is spending inefficiently and should be scrutinized.

## Why It Is the Catch-All Metric
Sacks argues the Burn Multiple is a catch-all because any serious problem will eventually show up in it, by increasing burn, decreasing net new ARR, or, most trickily, increasing both but at disproportionate rates. Unlike the Magic Number (which isolates sales-and-marketing efficiency) or gross-margin analysis (which isolates cost of goods), the Burn Multiple captures inefficiency anywhere in the business: bloated overhead, weak retention, discounting, or churn all degrade it. It effectively inverts Bessemer's Efficiency Score (Net New ARR over Net Burn) so that lower is better and it reads like a cost-of-growth multiplier. He also contrasts it with the Hype Ratio (total capital raised divided by ARR), which flags companies that raised far more than their revenue justifies.

## How To Use It
Because it holistically reflects capital efficiency, the Burn Multiple is a fast diagnostic in board and fundraising conversations: it tells an investor how many dollars of dilution-funded cash it takes to buy a dollar of durable recurring revenue. Improving it means either cutting net burn without stalling growth, or accelerating net new ARR (through better win rates, pricing, expansion, and retention) without proportionally raising spend.

title: Brad Feld, The Rule of 40% For a Healthy SaaS Company
text:
## The Rule of 40
The Rule of 40 states that a healthy SaaS company's growth rate plus its profit margin should add up to at least 40 percent. It is a late-stage investor test, most meaningful at scale (roughly $50M or more in revenue). The rule balances the two ways a SaaS company creates value: growth and profitability. A company can be highly profitable and grow slowly, or grow fast and burn, but the sum should clear 40.

## Worked Examples
If you are growing 20 percent, you should be generating about 20 percent profit (20 plus 20 equals 40). If you are growing 40 percent, you can be at roughly break-even, zero percent profit (40 plus 0 equals 40). If you are growing 50 percent, you can afford to lose about 10 percent (50 minus 10 equals 40). The faster you grow, the more loss the rule tolerates, because rapid growth is itself a form of value creation.

## Which Profit Metric
Defining profit is the tricky part. Feld prefers to use EBITDA as the baseline and then back-test with the other percentages. The right metric depends on the business: cloud-based companies have a simpler calculation, while companies running their own infrastructure must account for equipment purchases, debt, and lease expenses, which drive divergence between EBITDA, operating income, and net income. Later formulations of the rule often substitute free cash flow margin for profit. For the growth side, he recommends year-over-year MRR growth rate as the clearest measure, acknowledging ARR and other variants exist.

## How To Apply It
The Rule of 40 is a sanity check, not a target to optimize in isolation. A company far below 40 is either growing too slowly for the losses it is taking or burning too much for the growth it is buying. A company well above 40 may be under-investing in growth. Used correctly it forces an honest trade-off conversation between the growth and efficiency levers rather than celebrating growth at any cost.

title: Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million
text:
## CAC Payback Period
CAC Payback Period is the rate at which the costs spent to acquire a customer are repaid by that customer, and it usually includes sales, marketing, and customer success expenses. Bessemer's target thresholds vary by segment: SMB-focused companies should target under 12 months, mid-market-focused under 18 months, and enterprise-focused under 24 months. Longer payback is acceptable for larger, stickier enterprise contracts because those customers retain and expand for years.

## Gross Margin Targets
Investors expect cloud gross margins to stay within a fairly tight band of roughly 60 to 80 percent. Bessemer benchmarks: early stage ($1M to $10M ARR) around 70 percent; mid-stage ($10M to $50M ARR) 65 to 70 percent; scale stage ($50M+ ARR) 65 to 70 percent. Persistently low gross margin signals a services-heavy or infrastructure-heavy business masquerading as software.

## Net Revenue Retention and Gross Retention
Net Revenue Retention (also Net Dollar Retention, NDR) measures revenue from the existing customer base over time including expansion, minus contraction and churn. A good gross retention baseline is 85 to 90 percent across all scales. Great net retention is 120 percent or more; the middle of the pack exceeds 100 percent. Typical net retention runs 105 to 145 percent at $1M to $10M ARR, declining toward 105 to 125 percent by $100M+ ARR as the base matures. Gross retention can never exceed 100 percent (it only counts losses), while net retention above 100 percent means the base grows on its own.

## Rule of 40 and Growth Endurance
Bessemer expresses the Rule of 40 as free cash flow margin plus year-over-year ARR growth rate should equal 40 percent or more, and notes the average efficiency score across the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index is closer to 50 percent for the best public names. Growth endurance is the idea that a company retains only about 70 percent of its prior year's growth rate each year, so a company growing 100 percent this year should plan for roughly 70 percent next year.

## ARR Growth Benchmarks by Scale
Average ARR growth rates decline predictably with scale: about 200 percent at $1M to $10M ARR, about 115 percent at $10M to $25M, about 95 percent at $25M to $50M, and about 60 percent at $50M to $100M+. Bessemer's classic growth ideal for a breakout cloud company is Triple, Triple, Double, Double, Double (T2D3): triple revenue two years running, then double it for three years, which takes a company from roughly $2M to $100M+ ARR.

title: Klipfolio, SaaS Magic Number (Sales Efficiency)
text:
## SaaS Magic Number Definition
The SaaS Magic Number is a sales-efficiency ratio that indicates how much new recurring revenue a company generates for each dollar spent on sales and marketing, and therefore whether its go-to-market motion is sustainable. It answers a simple question: for every dollar poured into sales and marketing last quarter, how many dollars of annualized new revenue came back.

## Formula
SaaS Magic Number = ((Current quarter's GAAP revenue minus Previous quarter's GAAP revenue) times 4) divided by Previous quarter's sales and marketing spend. Multiplying the quarterly revenue increase by 4 annualizes it, and dividing by the prior quarter's spend attributes the new revenue to the investment that produced it (sales and marketing spend leads revenue by roughly a quarter).

## Interpretation Thresholds
Below 0.75 indicates the company is investing more in sales and marketing than it is earning back in recurring revenue in a reasonable window; it warrants a careful look at cash runway before spending more. A value of 0.75 or above shows the business generates more recurring customer income than it spends acquiring it, suggesting efficient acquisition and room to invest further to accelerate growth. Less than 0.5 often signals a flawed model or insufficient product-market fit that must be fixed before scaling spend. Greater than 0.75 is a positive signal to investors of solid sales-and-marketing efficiency, product-market fit, and effective monetization. The common rule of thumb: below about 0.75 pull back and fix efficiency, at or above 1.0 step on the gas.

## How To Use It and Its Limits
The Magic Number isolates sales-and-marketing efficiency, unlike the Burn Multiple which captures whole-company efficiency. Its weaknesses: it uses total revenue (not just new ARR, so churn and one-time revenue can distort it), it assumes a one-quarter lag between spend and revenue, and it is noisy quarter to quarter for small companies. Use it as a trend, not a single-point verdict, and pair it with CAC payback and retention.

title: SaaS Capital, What Is a Good Retention Rate for a Private SaaS Company
text:
## Net Revenue Retention vs Gross Revenue Retention
Net Revenue Retention (NRR) is calculated as the MRR in the current period (for example December 2024) coming only from customers who were already customers twelve months earlier (December 2023), divided by the total MRR from that earlier period. NRR includes the positive effects of upsells, cross-sells, and price increases, so NRR can exceed 100 percent. Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) uses the same formula but excludes all expansion (upsells, cross-sells, price increases); it captures only what you lost to churn and downgrades, so gross retention cannot exceed 100 percent. The gap between NRR and GRR is the contribution of expansion revenue.

## Benchmark by ACV
SaaS Capital emphasizes that companies which share a similar selling price (ACV) have the most in common, so benchmarking retention by ACV beats benchmarking by age, revenue, or industry. Median NRR increases with ACV: higher-priced solutions correlate with stronger retention because they involve longer sales cycles, deeper implementation, and dedicated account management, which make the product stickier and harder to rip out. For the $25,000 to $50,000 ACV band, median NRR is 102 percent, with the top quartile at 111 percent and the bottom quartile at 97 percent. Companies with the highest ACVs also show the highest gross retention rates.

## Retention Drives Growth
The data reveals a strong and exponential correlation between net revenue retention and growth. Among surveyed companies above $1M ARR, median growth was 24 percent, and companies achieving NRR of 110 percent or more exceeded the population medians. The practical lesson: retention is not a defensive metric, it is the single largest compounding lever on growth and valuation, because a high-NRR base grows revenue before a single new customer is added, and every point of retained revenue is far cheaper than newly acquired revenue.

## Anti-Pattern: Hiding Behind Net Retention
A company can post a healthy NRR above 100 percent while its gross retention is quietly poor, because a handful of large expanding accounts mask heavy logo and dollar churn underneath. Always read NRR and GRR together: strong NRR with weak GRR (for example NRR 110 percent but GRR 80 percent) means the business is leaking customers and papering over it with expansion from a few accounts, a fragile position if those accounts ever slow down.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, How the 3 Financial Statements Are Linked
text:
## The Three Statements
A complete financial model links the income statement (revenue, expenses, net income over a period), the balance sheet (assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time, where Assets = Liabilities + Equity always), and the cash flow statement (cash from operations, investing, and financing over a period). A three-statement model connects all three dynamically so a change in one assumption ripples correctly through all three.

## Net Income Linkage
Net income from the bottom of the income statement links to both the balance sheet and the cash flow statement. On the balance sheet, net income feeds into retained earnings (Retained Earnings = beginning balance plus net income minus dividends). On the cash flow statement, net income is the starting point for the cash from operations section.

## Depreciation and PP&E
Depreciation flows out of Property, Plant and Equipment (PP&E) on the balance sheet onto the income statement as an expense, and then is added back to net income in the cash flow statement (because it is a non-cash expense). Capital expenditures affect both the PP&E account on the balance sheet and the investing section of the cash flow statement.

## Working Capital
Changes in current assets (like accounts receivable and inventory) and current liabilities (like accounts payable) flow from the balance sheet into the operating section of the cash flow statement, increasing or reducing operating cash. Growing receivables consume cash; growing payables release cash.

## The Cash Balance Ties It Together
The sum of cash from operations, cash from investing, and cash from financing is added to the prior period's closing cash balance, and the result becomes the current period's closing cash balance on the balance sheet. This final step is what makes the balance sheet balance and ties all three statements together. In practice you forecast the income statement first, build supporting schedules (depreciation, debt/interest, working capital), complete the balance sheet except for cash, then let the cash flow statement solve for the ending cash line last. A driver-based model expresses each line as a function of an operating driver (revenue as units times price, headcount cost as heads times fully-loaded cost, and so on) rather than a blind growth percentage, so the model reflects the real business and can be flexed for scenarios.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Cash Runway Explained
text:
## Cash Runway
Cash runway is the number of months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash, holding spending roughly constant. The formula is: Cash Runway = Current Cash Balance divided by Monthly Net Burn Rate. When runway approaches zero the company hits its zero-cash date, the calendar month it becomes insolvent unless it raises, cuts burn, or reaches cash-flow breakeven first.

## Gross Burn vs Net Burn
Gross burn rate is total monthly cash expenses (rent, salaries, overhead, all cash outflows). Net burn rate is monthly cash sales minus monthly cash expenses, that is, the net amount of cash the company consumes each month after its own revenue offsets some of the spending. Net burn is the number that matters for runway, because incoming revenue extends the time the cash lasts.

## Worked Example
A startup has $250,000 in the bank. It spends $90,000 per month and brings in $20,000 per month, so net burn = $90,000 minus $20,000 = $70,000 per month. Cash Runway = $250,000 divided by $70,000, which is approximately 3.6 months. That means, at the current rate, the company runs out of cash in about three and a half months and must act well before then.

## Why It Matters
Runway drives every major decision: when to raise, how aggressively to hire, and when to cut. A common operating rule is to raise before runway falls under about 6 months (fundraising itself takes months) and to target 18 to 24 months of runway after a round so the team can hit the milestones that justify the next raise. The two ways to extend runway are to reduce net burn (cut costs, delay hiring) or to grow cash revenue faster than cash costs. Watch the trend in net burn month over month, not just a single snapshot, because a rising burn rate shortens runway faster than the static formula implies.

title: ChartMogul, SaaS Metrics Cheat Sheet
text:
## MRR and Its Movements
Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) is the normalized monthly value of subscriptions: MRR = amount paid for a subscription item divided by the number of months in the plan interval (so an annual plan is spread across 12 months, not booked all at once). MRR is the foundation of SaaS financial analysis, and its value is in decomposing the change each month into movements. New business MRR is new recurring revenue from newly converted customers. Expansion MRR is added revenue from existing customers upgrading or buying add-ons. Contraction MRR is revenue lost when existing customers downgrade or drop add-ons. Churn MRR is revenue from subscriptions canceled in the period. Reactivation MRR is revenue from previously churned customers returning to a paid plan. Net New MRR = New plus Expansion plus Reactivation minus Contraction minus Churn. Tracking these five movements separately is what turns a single MRR number into a diagnosis.

## ARPA
Average Revenue Per Account (ARPA) = total revenue in a period divided by the number of customers in the same period. It drives pricing decisions and is a key input to LTV and CAC analysis.

## Customer Churn vs Revenue Churn
Customer churn rate is the percentage of customers who cancel in a period. Revenue churn is the percentage of revenue lost through cancellations and downgrades. These can differ significantly depending on how revenue is distributed: losing many tiny customers hurts customer churn more than revenue churn, while losing one whale hurts revenue churn far more. Always look at both.

## Net MRR Churn and Benchmarks
Net MRR Churn Rate = (Churn MRR plus Contraction MRR minus Expansion MRR minus Reactivation MRR) divided by MRR at the start of the period. Negative net MRR churn (expansion outweighs losses) is the gold standard. Benchmark medians by ARR stage: under $300k ARR around 6.2 percent, $1M to $3M around 2.3 percent, $15M to $30M around 1.8 percent; churn should fall as the company matures and moves upmarket.

## Cohort Analysis
A cohort is simply a group; in SaaS, cohort analysis follows customers who joined in the same period (say, all January signups) and tracks their retained revenue and behavior month by month afterward. Cohort curves reveal whether retention stabilizes (a flattening curve is healthy) and whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones (evidence the product and onboarding are improving). Cohort-based revenue retention is the honest way to see churn, because a blended company-wide churn number can be flattered by a flood of new signups masking decay in the older base.

title: CRV, Equity Dilution Explained: A Founder's Guide
text:
## Pre-Money and Post-Money Valuation
The foundational identity: post-money valuation equals pre-money valuation plus the investment amount. From it flow the two calculations that matter in a priced round: investor ownership percentage equals investment amount divided by post-money valuation, and price per share equals pre-money valuation divided by pre-money fully diluted shares. A negotiation quoted in pre-money terms and one quoted in post-money terms are not the same deal at the same headline number; always convert to ownership percentage before agreeing.

## Ownership and Dilution
Dilution is the reduction in each existing holder's ownership percentage when new shares are issued. Ownership acquired by new investors equals investment divided by post-money. Across rounds, dilution compounds multiplicatively: a founder's remaining stake is the product of (1 minus the dilution) at each round. CRV cites that the median founding team retains about 56.2 percent after their seed round, roughly 36.1 percent after Series A, and around 23 percent after Series B, illustrating how ownership erodes as each round adds shareholders.

## The Option Pool and the Option Pool Shuffle
Early-stage employee option pools commonly land in the 10 to 15 percent range of fully diluted shares. The timing of pool creation has a large economic effect. When investors specify a required post-money option pool percentage, the shares needed to reach that percentage are created before the investment closes, so the pool is carved from the founders' side of the table: founders absorb the entire dilution of the pool while the investor's target ownership stays unchanged. This is the option pool shuffle. Modeling it is essential, because a larger pre-money pool is economically identical to a lower pre-money valuation for the founders.

## The Finance Analyst's Job Here
Before accepting any term sheet, model the exact fully diluted cap table and each holder's post-round ownership, including the option pool expansion, at several valuation and pool-size assumptions. The right output is a sensitivity table of founder ownership versus pre-money valuation and pool size, so the team negotiates on true ownership and cost of capital, not the headline valuation.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Contribution Margin Overview
text:
## Contribution Margin
Contribution margin is a business's sales revenue less its variable costs. The resulting amount is what is available to cover fixed costs; any excess becomes profit. Formula: Contribution Margin = Net Sales Revenue minus Variable Costs (equivalently, Contribution Margin = Fixed Costs plus Net Income). The contribution margin ratio = (Net Sales Revenue minus Variable Costs) divided by Sales Revenue, expressed as a percentage. Contribution margin is distinct from gross margin: it strips out only the variable costs, isolating how much each incremental sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit.

## Break-Even Analysis
Because fixed costs are usually large, the contribution margin must be high enough to cover the cost of operating the business. The break-even point is where total contribution margin exactly equals fixed costs, so profit is zero. Break-even in units = Fixed Costs divided by Contribution Margin per unit. A low contribution margin can indicate an unprofitable product line that does not earn enough per sale to justify its fixed-cost base.

## Worked Example
A phone manufacturer sells 50,000 units at $100 each with $40 of total variable cost per unit. Contribution margin per unit = $100 minus $40 = $60. Total contribution margin = $60 times 50,000 = $3 million. Contribution margin ratio = $60 divided by $100 = 60 percent. If the company's fixed costs were, say, $1.8 million, break-even units = $1,800,000 divided by $60 = 30,000 units, so every unit beyond 30,000 drops $60 to the bottom line.

## Why It Matters for a Startup
Contribution margin per customer (revenue minus the variable cost to serve) is the correct numerator for LTV, and it is the number that must eventually exceed CAC for the unit economics to work. Break-even analysis tells the team how much volume, or what price, is required before the business funds its own fixed cost base, which is the bridge between unit economics and the path to profitability.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Variance Analysis (FP&A)
text:
## What Variance Analysis Is
Variance analysis is the analysis of the difference between planned (budgeted or standard) and actual numbers. It is the core feedback loop of FP&A (financial planning and analysis): you set a budget or forecast, you measure actuals, and you explain the gap so it can be fixed or exploited. The goal is to identify a problem so it can be corrected, or simply to improve overall company performance.

## Favorable vs Unfavorable
A variance is favorable when actual results are better than plan (for example, actual cost lower than the standard cost of raw materials, or actual revenue above budget). A variance is unfavorable when actuals are worse than plan (for example, the standard quantity was 10,000 pieces of material but 15,000 were required, consuming more resources than expected). Favorable and unfavorable are about direction relative to plan, not simply higher or lower.

## Types of Variance
Variances decompose into a price/rate component and a quantity/efficiency component. For materials, labor, and variable overhead: the price/rate variance compares actual cost per unit against the standard, and the quantity/efficiency variance compares the volume of input used against the standard. Fixed overhead splits into budget and volume variances instead. Decomposing a total variance into price versus volume tells you whether you missed on how much you paid or on how much you used, which point to different fixes.

## How FP&A Uses It
Management reviews significant variances (usually those above a materiality threshold or percentage) each period, explains the driver, and feeds the learning into the next forecast (a rolling forecast or reforecast). Good FP&A does not just report the variance, it attributes it to a business driver (price, volume, mix, timing, or one-time items) and recommends an action. This is the discipline that turns a static annual budget into a living operating plan, and it is what separates a finance analyst who narrates the past from one who steers the business.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Scenario Analysis
text:
## Scenario Analysis
Scenario analysis is the process of examining and evaluating possible future events or scenarios and predicting the various feasible outcomes. In a financial model you build discrete scenarios, each a self-consistent set of assumptions (product prices, customer metrics, operating costs, inflation, interest rates, and other business drivers) changed together, and observe how the outputs (revenue, burn, runway, cash) respond.

## The Three Standard Cases
Models typically carry three cases. The base case is the average scenario built on management's assumptions, the plan you actually run against. The worst case (downside) considers the most serious or severe outcome that could occur, for example slower growth, higher churn, and a delayed raise. The best case (upside) is the ideal projected scenario management would pursue if everything breaks right. Presenting all three forces an honest conversation about the range of outcomes rather than a single point estimate.

## Scenario vs Sensitivity Analysis
Scenario analysis changes a coherent bundle of assumptions at once to describe a whole possible world (a recession case, a fast-growth case). Sensitivity analysis instead flexes one input at a time (say, monthly churn or CAC) to see how much the output moves, isolating which single variable the model is most sensitive to. Scenario analysis answers 'what if this whole situation happens,' sensitivity analysis answers 'which assumption matters most.' A rigorous model uses both: sensitivity to find the high-leverage drivers, scenarios to stress the plan.

## Why It Matters
Scenario and sensitivity analysis give founders and investors insight into expected returns and the risks involved, let a business assess investment prospects, and allow the company to proactively avoid or decrease potential losses under unfavorable conditions. For a startup the most important scenario question is usually 'in the downside case, when do we run out of cash, and what do we cut first,' which turns modeling into a survival plan rather than an academic exercise.

title: CloudZero, SaaS COGS: What To Include In Your Cost Of Goods Sold
text:
## What Belongs in SaaS Cost of Revenue (COGS)
For a SaaS business, COGS (cost of revenue) is the cost of delivering and supporting the service to existing customers, not the cost of building or selling it. Include: cloud infrastructure and hosting (for example AWS, EC2, and S3 bills), customer support personnel (salaries, training, onboarding), DevOps and production engineering labor (the engineers who keep production running), third-party software licenses and subscriptions that directly support running the service, transactional and payment processing costs, and professional services / implementation labor and tooling. Customer success tied to serving and retaining existing customers generally belongs here too.

## What Does NOT Belong in COGS
Exclude research and development (building new product), sales and marketing and all customer acquisition costs, general and administrative overhead and management functions, depreciation and amortization of intangibles, and interest and financing costs. Misclassifying any of these is how companies flatter their gross margin.

## Gross Margin Formula and Benchmarks
Gross Profit = Total Revenue minus COGS. As a percentage, COGS percent = (COGS divided by Total Revenue) times 100, and gross margin is its inverse (if COGS is 23 percent of revenue, gross margin is 77 percent). Healthy SaaS targets COGS at 15 to 30 percent of revenue, implying 70 to 85 percent gross margins; the industry median total gross margin is around 77 percent. Companies consistently below 70 percent total gross margin warrant investigation, because they may be more services or infrastructure business than software.

## Anti-Pattern: Inflating Gross Margin and Confusing Margins
A classic manipulation is to move real costs of serving customers (hosting, support, customer success, DevOps) out of COGS and into operating expense or R&D, which artificially inflates gross margin. A faithful analyst insists on a consistent, complete COGS definition. Also do not confuse the margins: gross margin subtracts only cost of revenue; contribution margin subtracts variable costs; operating (net) margin subtracts all operating expenses including sales, marketing, R&D, and G&A. A company can show a beautiful 80 percent gross margin and still burn heavily because sales, marketing, and R&D below the gross-profit line consume it all. Gross margin is a statement about the product's unit economics; net margin is a statement about the whole business.
